blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Jury in, please.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (In the presence of the jury)
Good morning, members of the jury.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you all for coming in today. If any of you don't feel well at any stage, please just make that known to me, but otherwise we'll just proceed as normal.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: May I call Dr Stephen Brearey, please.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: DR STEPHEN BREAREY (sworn)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you please state your full name for the record?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Stephen Paul Brearey.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Dr Brearey, during the course of asking you questions, I'll be drawing your attention to some clinical notes that were made by both yourself and colleagues and they will appear on the screen immediately to your right for your point of reference. I know that you will have anticipated you've been invited here today to provide evidence in relation to your involvement with the care of a baby by the name of [Baby G] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- who I think, this is right, could you confirm, is still a child in relation to whom you have a continuing professional relationship?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We know, and I remind you if I may, that [Baby G] was admitted into the neonatal unit at the Countess of Chester Hospital from Arrowe Park Hospital on 14 August 2015.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Prior to giving evidence here this morning, have you been given and taken the opportunity to remind yourself of the contents of the notes pertaining to her time within the NNU at Chester over the following several weeks?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, I have.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Might I ask you to address your answers to the jury to best aid communication.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I'm confident I can lead you in this regard. Did you first review [Baby G] on 22 August 2015 --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- during a ward round?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Did you then review her again on 2 September 2015 during your on-call week?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Are you able to inform the jury in general terms about how she was on those two occasions and what, if any, developments had occurred during the week and a half or so between reviewing her on your rounds?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So on the 22nd, she had already been on the neonatal unit for over a week and the general trend was one of improvements. The main medical concerns were her respiratory support; she had chronic lung disease of prematurity. When she arrived to Chester on 14 August, I believe, she was on CPAP, continuous positive airway pressure, and in a reasonable amount of oxygen. By the time I saw her on the 22nd, that had been weaned successfully to humidified high-flow oxygen, Optiflow, and her oxygen requirement had come down a little.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The general impression was one of improvement in her respiratory status and she was establishing feeds.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: There had been a long-term issue in terms of her having a full abdomen, which isn't unusual for babies born this early, and I think I prescribed or suggested a prescription for a suppository to help her move her bowels on the 22nd, which was successful. But otherwise there was no changes to her management and no concerns.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Then in September, when I saw her on the Wednesday, I believe, again there was a pattern of improvement.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Her flow rate for Optiflow had come down. Everything was moving in the right direction. She continued to establish enteral feeds and I believe, if it wasn't on that day it might have been later that week, she'd started to take bottles as well as NG feeds.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. So that takes us into the early part of September 2015. Now I'm going to invite you to focus your attention more specifically on the 6th and 7 September.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To assist you in that regard, we will look at the notes that you and a colleague or two made at around that time.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So if I ask Mr Murphy to put on screen, please, our tile 28. This presentation has been created for the benefit of the jury to provide a chronology of the events and you see your name there and a reference to clinical notes made at 11 am on Sunday, 6 September, and we'll click on and you'll be shown, firstly, a summary of what's contained within your actual notes and then we'll now present the note itself to you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Do you recognise that as your handwriting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Timed and dated 11 am, 6 September 2015. In what context did you create this clinical note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It was a Sunday morning. I was the consultant on that weekend and I saw [Baby G] and reviewed her on the ward round, on the neonatal ward rounds. [Baby G] was a corrected gestation of 38 weeks, corrected gestation, so was considered to be term, corrected. And as I have said, the main medical diagnoses were chronic lung disease of prematurity and mild bilateral ventriculomegaly, which is -- the ventricles of the brain were slightly enlarged on cranial ultrasound scans.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there, so a corrected gestational age because she was in fact born at a gestation of 23 weeks and 6 days as your note informs --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: However, 97 days had passed since that event.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And therefore adding the two together, she was effectively a term baby by now?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Take us through your next recorded note, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So systematically, looking at her respiratory or ventilation status, she was on low-flow oxygen, so that's a step down from the Optiflow that she'd been on previously. And she was receiving 0.06 litres a minute of nasal cannula oxygen, which is a very small amount of oxygen. The nurses had not reported any significant desaturations, drops in her oxygen levels, from the notes that I reviewed -- from the nurse notes that I reviewed that morning.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: From a fluid and cardiovascular point of view she was receiving 180ml per kilo per day of milk. This was mother's expressed breast milk. It was being given via the nasogastric tube in addition to some bottles. So clearly, she was making progress with that if she was taking bottles of milk at that time. And her oxygen requirement was coming down. Things looked quite stable and improving.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there, can you assist us as to an appreciation of the volume? So 180ml, is that in total per day or is that per kilo of her weight?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's per kilo of her weight. You can see underneath her weight at the time was 1.985 kilograms, almost 2 kilograms, so she would have been receiving in a 24-hour period roughly 360ml in that 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you guide the jury as to that weight as per a baby with a corrected gestational age of 38 weeks? Is that around the target weight or is she still a little under?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was still a little under. It's not uncommon for preterm babies that they -- the target for us is really for them
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: to catch up some weight so that they end up on a normal centile line and particularly she'd had quite a stormy time at Arrowe Park Hospital. One of the reasons that she's on 180ml per kilogram per day was -- the normal for a preterm baby at this stage would normally be 150ml per kilogram per day, but clinical staff will often go up to 180ml per kilogram per day to help promote growth when the baby is tolerating the milk and it's beneficial for those babies.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. I interrupted you. You were telling us that that was 180ml per kilo weight of expressed breast milk.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And then the next line indicates?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So [Baby G] was on Gaviscon and fortifier. So the fortifier is a breast milk fortifier which gives a little extra in the way of calories but also gives some extra vitamins as well. The Gaviscon written in the note there is a reflux treatment to help -- it actually lines the -- it's an alginate that covers the lining of the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's input?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. And the output then would be that she was passing urine satisfactorily. She'd opened her bowels. Her weight had increased to 1.985 kilos.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You confirmed a minute or two ago that from a respiration perspective, it was a positive trend?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And from a feeding and digestive perspective, how were things going with [Baby G] in the 15 days or so that she'd been under your care?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Still receiving a little more milk than average to boost the calories and her growth, but tolerating this well.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Her gut was clearly working normally because she was opening her bowels and there were no nursing concerns in that respect.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Next is a list of meds that she was receiving, some of which you've already alluded to, certainly the Gaviscon.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The Gaviscon I've just mentioned. The two medicines are furosemide and spironolactone, which are both diuretics, which are given, in this case, for chronic lung disease of prematurity and often help reduce the requirement for oxygen for preterm babies. A side effect of diuretics is that you sometimes lose
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: salts in the urine and that's why [Baby G] was on sodium chloride supplements to treat that.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Then on examination?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: On examination she appeared pink and well. Her heart sounds were normal. No murmurs were heard. Her chest was clear on auscultation -- that's listening to the chest -- and her abdomen that morning appeared soft.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Therefore the plan was?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To continue with establishing feeds, taking more bottles and less NG tubes, that would mean. When babies get close to considering discharge at this term/gestation that she's at, then because she had chronic lung disease of prematurity, she'd be considered as a high risk for RSV bronchiolitis, which is a viral chest infection, so for those high-risk babies, after they go home, they have a monthly injection of palivizumab, which is a type of vaccine to prevent bronchiolitis.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So this was one of the preparatory steps in anticipation of her discharge to home?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. So that was your examination of [Baby G] and your projected plan as of the morning of 6 September?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What was the nature of your duties on 7 September?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was the on-call consultant that day, so obviously it involves some ward work during the daytime and then I would be the on-call consultant overnight until 8.30 the following morning.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And were you called in in the early hours of 7 September?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: By whom and in what circumstances?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dr Ventress, the registrar on overnight, called me in at approximately 3.30, I believe.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Did you attend at the NNU and did you attend upon [Baby G] at that time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And was Dr Ventress there at your arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was present, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And were you at that point appraised by Dr Ventress of the events that had caused her to call you in?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was just at the point of intubating [Baby G] when I arrived, but obviously would have explained things afterwards, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. I wonder whether Mr Murphy -- there are notes from Dr Ventress and Dr Brearey behind a single tile. Can we go to that rather than hopping about from tile to tile?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We can see notes here made by Dr Ventress which, if we continue to look at them, include reference to the fact that you were called in and appraised of the situation. So you were called in because [Baby G], it was said, had had a very large projectile vomit and you told us a minute or two ago that, at the point of your arrival, [Baby G] was being intubated or Dr Ventress was attempting to intubate [Baby G]. Can you tell us what you recall of the situation upon your arrival?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, Dr Ventress explained to me, as you can see in the record, that she'd been called urgently to [Baby G] because she had had this very large projectile vomit, which -- some of it landed on the chair next to the cot as well as the canopy. This seems quite unusual now looking at this in retrospect. It's not something that I have witnessed before.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there, you have not witnessed any projectile vomiting or this sort of projectile vomiting?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, I have witnessed projectile vomiting in babies with other diagnoses, but in a preterm baby like this who's been stable for so long without the diagnosis of something called pyloric stenosis, I haven't witnessed this ever before, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Without digressing too far, you said without the diagnosis of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Pyloric stenosis is a condition that usually affects term babies and is a narrowing in the muscle at the base of the stomach and develops around about 2 months of age and causes classical projectile vomiting. It's clear that [Baby G] didn't have this diagnosis from her history and the lack of vomiting prior to this episode.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So I can't remember -- I haven't mentioned in my statement and I can't remember Dr Ventress mentioning the discoloured purple abdomen, but [Baby G] had -- was known to be having a distended stomach previously on occasion.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: And Dr Ventress felt in her initial review that [Baby G] was getting back to normal again after the initial call, but then went to the preterm delivery room, was called back urgently when [Baby G] had further -- had a further desaturation and bradycardia, a dropping of the heart rate, and Dr Ventress had made the decision to intubate [Baby G] and had finished intubating [Baby G] or was in the process of that when I arrived.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So just to recap on history, was it relayed to you Dr Ventress was called to look at [Baby G] post the projectile vomit?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Shortly thereafter, Dr Ventress was called elsewhere --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- to assist with a delivery and then recalled to [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And it was at that point that you -- or shortly thereafter -- first attended on [Baby G] this morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Were you called in from home or were you doing something else within the NNU at that point?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I was called in from home.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. How was [Baby G] at the point that you encountered her on the early hours of 7 September?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Initially, it appeared from the observations that she had stabilised after intubation. I can see from my statement that I've made a comment about the gas that occurred half an hour after the intubation, which appeared normal, actually. Following from writing this statement, I realised that I was actually called to the preterm delivery that Dr Ventress had been called away from to attend to [Baby G], and that baby was
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: born at around about 4 am, so there was a period of time when I was in delivery suite attending to that other preterm delivery.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you came in from home, you went to [Baby G], but at some point thereafter your services were required elsewhere?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can remember being satisfied that Dr Ventress had the situation in control with [Baby G] once she'd intubated and clearly the monitors were acceptable, you know, the readings, and then I needed to go to the other preterm delivery, on the delivery suite, but I'm aware that a gas was done half an hour later after the intubation and that showed that -- that was effectively normal.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I wonder if we could scroll down to Dr Brearey's contribution to the notes. I'm sorry, having asked you to do that, towards the bottom of the screen we can see Dr Ventress recorded Dr Brearey in attendance.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: If we just consider Dr Ventress' note from that point onwards.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So the ventilator settings, pressure of 18/5, and a rate of 40, and inspired oxygen concentration of 30%, I'd consider to be relatively low ventilator settings, which means at that time [Baby G] wasn't difficult to ventilate and actually when we reviewed the gas 30 minutes after the intubation, we reduced the pressures down to 16/5.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So even within half an hour, her ventilation status was satisfactory, allowing us to wean her ventilation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Then in the chronology we get to 5.30 or thereabouts, as Dr Ventress recorded:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "At approximately 5.30, [Baby G] had another profound desaturation."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is that the second event that you are referring to?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes, exactly. Yes. So her heart rate dropped to 60 and oxygen levels dropped to 40%. On a ventilator, again this is unusual, and I suppose the first question a clinician would ask themselves is: is the ventilator providing the support that we're asking it to provide?
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: To be completely safe, Dr Ventress took [Baby G] off the ventilator to provide support by a more manual method, using the Neopuff, which is a device to provide pressurised oxygen to [Baby G]. The capnograph was still connected and that was still changing colour, which suggests that the endotracheal tube was still in the correct position. The chest movement was
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: satisfactory for Dr Ventress, so -- can you just scroll to the top of that, sorry?
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So [Baby G] recovered slowly from that desaturation and was reattached to the ventilator. Again, there was some uncertainty at this time regarding the ventilator and it was changed for another ventilator. It would appear that the leak that the first ventilator was alarming to was still present in the second ventilator, which tells me that it wasn't a ventilator problem if a ventilator had been changed and there's still the same issue.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there if you would for a moment, can you assist the jury as to that issue by defining what a leak is and giving it some context?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So in adult ventilation, the tube that goes into the trachea, into the airway, has a little balloon around it as it enters the airway to stop any gas escaping so that everything the ventilator puts into the lungs is used to expand the lungs. Those balloons traditionally haven't been used in babies, in preterm babies, because the pressure of the balloon that stops or seals the leak, if you like, can then damage the airway of preterm babies.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So neonates at this time were intubated with uncuffed tubes that would always have some degree of leak. A small degree of leak is fine. A large degree of leak might indicate that your tube is too small and you need a slightly larger tube. But we wouldn't change to a larger tube if the baby was ventilating satisfactorily. So if their chest was moving and the gases were normal, even with a larger leak, you'd still be happy with that and feel that was satisfactory.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you for that. So there was a change in equipment, but a large leak remained, according to the notes. And if that is not a consequence of some flaw in equipment, what's the explanation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I can't explain that explanation, actually. It's unusual for babies to desaturate on a ventilator, particularly in view of the normal gas that they had or [Baby G] had prior to that. It doesn't -- and the fact that Dr Ventress was getting chest movement when she was Neopuffing the baby off the ventilator. It's perplexing and I can't think of a natural cause why that would happen.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Can we move to Dr Ventress' note at 06.05.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So [Baby G] had a further desaturation to 40% oxygen levels and her heart rate dropped to 80. Dr Ventress made the
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: decision to re-intubate with a larger ET tube. I was around at this time, I can remember. So she's talked about the heart rate being 120, but sats remained 50, and we increased the PIP, which is the peak inspiratory pressure ventilator, to 26. The oxygen inspired oxygen level was then 100%. The endotracheal tube was removed at 06.10.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Dr Ventress noted thick secretions from the mouth and a blood clot at the end of the endotracheal tube.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: More intermittent positive pressure ventilation was given via the Neopuff -- sorry, via the face mask. Jaw thrusts and a Guedel -- Guedel is an airway adjunct to keep the airway patent in the upper part of the mouth and the pharynx. But despite this, there was poor chest movement and oxygen levels dropped to 17% and her heart rate to 70.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Pausing there, going back over that ground again in a little more detail, looking at the entry a few lines up which reads:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "IPPV given via ETT. Initially [and then an arrow].
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Heart rate 120. Blood sat remained 50 despite [(inaudible) arrow] PIP to 26 and 100% oxygen."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Could you please elaborate upon that and the use of the words "but" and "despite" in there which seem to suggest --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The IPPV, I assume, is Dr Ventress using the Neopuff rather than the ventilator to provide positive pressure through the ET tube. The heart rate was above 100, but the oxygen levels were low at 50 and the peak inspiratory pressure was increased to 26, so much higher pressure than initially [Baby G] needed, despite 100% oxygen.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So you'd normally expect a higher pressure that you're delivering and a higher oxygen level you're delivering to increase the oxygen levels for [Baby G] in the knowledge that the tube was in the correct position. So despite those extra measures, [Baby G]'s oxygen levels were still not what you'd want.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So those were, at this point in time, those extra measures, resulting in the anticipated and desired consequences?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Were they or were they not? Were they working as expected?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The oxygen levels were lower than you would expect for those interventions.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving back to where I interrupted you, with apologies. So the face mask was being applied, jaw thrusts and a Guedel being used to enhance the respiratory support, is that correct --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- in summary? And notwithstanding that, there remained poor chest movement and the saturation levels, according to this note, continued to drop, is that right --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- now to 17% and now also her heart rate was dropping.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Was that a significant drop down to 70?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Certainly, yes. If you're below 100 you'd be concerned, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Therefore, according to the note, you were called in urgently. Can you pick up the thread from there if you would, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So the NG tube was aspirated and appeared very large, 100ml aspirated. It doesn't say 100ml of what, but I'm assuming milk and stomach fluid/contents.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: This seemed surprising because [Baby G] had been on a feed of 45ml, three-hourly and had already had a large vomit that covered the cot and the area round the cot, and had aspirated 45ml as well at that time and then again, when we hadn't fed [Baby G], having 100ml aspirated in the stomach really appears to be abnormal and I can't explain where that fluid would have come from.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But that would be something that would be standard practice in aspirating the stomach prior to a further intubation which was planned, because you'd want the stomach empty prior to intubation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So the aspiration was part of protocol, as it were?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But the results were surprising?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And that surprisingly large quantity of fluid, to put it neutrally, having been aspirated, thereafter did her sats gradually improve?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, she was re-intubated at 06.15 with a larger tube, the 3.5 tube, and that was a tight fit through the cords, as Dr Ventress has recorded. There was some bloodstained fluid in the oropharynx, she has noted.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: She suctioned below the cords, which means having a look at the vocal cords and passing a smaller suction catheter below the cords in case there's blood below the cords, in the actual airway itself, but nil was obtained from the area. So she can see blood in the oropharynx but not actually in the trachea.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Can you just help the jury with the distinction between the oropharynx and the trachea?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So the oropharynx is the upper airway and the oesophagus -- then splits into the oesophagus and then trachea, if you like, so the fact that she wasn't aspirating any -behind the cords in the trachea might have suggested the blood was coming from some other place, either the oesophagus or the oropharynx.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: She secured the ET tube at 8 centimetres at the lips, which it had been secured at before, so we knew the right position for the ET tube. And the capnograph was positive, which suggests that the ET tube was in the correct position. When listening with the stethoscope, we could hear a good air entry on both sides.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. A plan was formulated and discussed with you, according to Dr Ventress' note.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And could you expand upon the plan, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The plan was to give [Baby G] a pancuronium bolus, which is -- pancuronium is a medication to paralyse the baby to allow for better ventilation. So sometimes when babies are awake, they can breathe against the ventilator, which makes things more difficult, so usually a paralysing agent like pancuronium can help aid mechanical ventilation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The second bullet point for the plan was to repeat a blood gas in 30 minutes. The third was to continue with morphine at 30 micrograms per kilo per hour for sedation. [Baby G] was to be nil by mouth and IV fluids to be given and to prescribe cefotaxime, an antibiotic, to cover for any infection. And parents were or were about to be updated.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Let's just go through those bullet points again. You've explained the sedation was designed to make her more passive and aid the artificial ventilation.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The purpose of taking a gas in 30 minutes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: To assess how effectively we were ventilating her and whether there were any other signs that might explain the symptoms that we'd seen. It's standard practice to do this usually at that time after an intubation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: To continue with morphine; why?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again it's a similar reason for the pancuronium, so [Baby G] was settled, not in pain, and responded to the ventilator in a more effective way.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The next bullet point, the nutritional feeding regime?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, she'd had a huge vomit and a huge aspirate, so from a medical point of view we weren't sure at that time whether there was anything wrong with her gut and whilst we performed further investigations and got a better idea of what was causing this, it would be good practice to not give her any enteral milk.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. And other than informing her parents of the development, there's one more entry, cefotaxime. The purpose of introducing that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Cefotaxime is a broad spectrum antibiotic, which was standard practice on the unit at the time for treating late neonatal sepsis.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see alongside the plan, the bullet points and plan, there's a review of an X-ray undertaken by Dr Ventress. Did you review that X-ray, can you recall?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And what did it inform you of?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, I agreed with what's written there, that the lungs showed a typical picture of chronic lung disease of prematurity, which are diffuse patchy changes in both sides of the lungs, but that was known about previously.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: There wasn't -- there didn't seem to be anything new that was apparent on the chest X-ray that would explain the symptoms that had happened that night. And there was no evidence of any pneumothoraces, which again is a possible cause for sudden deterioration in a preterm baby. And as described by Dr Ventress, the abdomen had some generalised gaseous distension, but nothing that would indicate obstruction, which is another possible medical cause for vomiting. And nothing that would indicate necrotising enterocolitis, which would be very uncommon at this gestation anyway.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Mr Murphy, could we scroll further down the notes? We'll then see your handwriting I believe, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So a note made retrospectively, the note itself made at 8.15 that morning, which sets out, does it, in terms, that which you've just shared with the jury in your evidence?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So Dr Ventress shared the history with you and all of which, if we're looking down -- just explain to us, including the AXR, the abdominal X-ray, which is where we just got to, I think -- you tell us what it says, please, next to AXR, just where the cursor is.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes:
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "Gaseous abdomen, no perforation. Good air entry.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Good gas post-intubation."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That was the first intubation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right. No perforation, I don't think you mentioned that when taking us through the X-ray.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sorry. So necrotising enterocolitis, specifically in a severe form, can cause a perforation of the gut, so the gut is perforated and some gas then can escape from inside the bowel, and you can see evidence of gas outside the bowel, and there was no evidence of that either.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. Take us to 5.30, please, Mr Murphy.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So a fourth desaturation and bradycardia, as described by Dr Ventress, and as I've already discussed the change to a 3.5 size endotracheal tube, with less leak and better flow volume loops, that means for the F and the V loops. The ventilator has a flow sensor on it, which measures the flow of the gas in and out, and that gives (inaudible: coughing) loop with the inspiration and expiration and gives you an idea of the compliance of the lungs and the amount of leak and the ventilator was showing a better loop with the 3.5 tube than it did with the 3.0 tube.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. "Post-intubation"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Alongside the arrow, if we move the cursor down a line or two -- sorry, the gas, when it says "gas satisfactory", that's the results of a gas test were satisfactory?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What does it say after the word "satisfactory"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Compensated metabolic acidosis."
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: What does that mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Looking at the gas results and reading this, I think this might have been an error on my part after a fairly long night, that the pH was normal and, if anything, showing compensated respiratory acidosis rather than metabolic acidosis. That might be an error on my part, I'm afraid, at that time of day, sorry.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We asked for a 10ml per kilo fluid bolus and for some IV dopamine to be started, an infusion to be started. Both of those would be given to support blood pressure and I have justified that in the next two lines. [Baby G] had had a further bradycardia and looked poorly perfused at this time and therefore that was the indication for the fluid bolus and starting the dopamine.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. The next entry is sedation, which you've already told us about. And then for further gas examination, is that, at 9 am?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And:
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: "Will need to discuss with Arrowe Park/Liverpool Women's Hospital."
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Could you explain that entry to us, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Well, the designation of the unit we were at the time would allow for 48 hours of ventilation, but in addition, if the babies needed inotropic support in addition to mechanical ventilation, then the indication would be then that that baby is looked after in a neonatal intensive care unit such as Arrowe Park Hospital.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So that's a contemplation of what might be needed --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- in the immediate future?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And finally, her parents were kept up to date with events. Did that effectively conclude your direct involvement with [Baby G] on that date?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But as you indicated at the beginning of your evidence, you have continuing involvement with [Baby G] --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- as her general paediatric consultant?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And could you, in a sentence or two, inform the jury as to the main features of [Baby G]'s condition and health as time as moved on?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Okay. So [Baby G] had an MRI scan of her brain following these events, which looked worse than her previous MRI scan and I believe my colleague [Dr C], one of the consultants
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: in Chester, spoke to the parents at the time about the results of this. It's still uncertain at that early time what the longterm prognosis looked like for [Baby G], but over the months and years since then [Baby G] has developed dystonic quadriplegic cerebral palsy.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Break that down for us.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Cerebral palsy is a condition, usually as a result of brain damage in early life, that causes the arms and the legs and muscles of the body to be usually stiff and of very limited function. The dystonia is an additional factor in some babies with cerebral palsy and causes episodes of stiffness and abnormal movement in limbs and other muscles of the body, which can make things considerably worse.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's dystonia?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Dystonia, yes. In the first years of her life [Baby G] had a number of admissions to the paediatric intensive care unit for problems with aspiration and with chest infections that required further mechanical ventilation.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: She initially started with a gastrostomy, which is a tube inserted directly into the stomach to have liquid feed, because she wasn't considered to have a safe swallow. That has since been changed into a gastrojejunostomy tube, so the tube goes further down the gut, which means that the food that she has is less likely to be aspirated and she's less likely to have chest infections.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So she is completely dependent on the care of her parents, who give an incredible level of care to her, and I have great respect for everything they have done for her over the last 6 or so years.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When you spoke a sentence or two ago about the risk of food being aspirated, in this context what does aspiration mean?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Aspiration in that context means stomach contents coming up from the stomach and, because her swallow and gag reflex isn't what most people have, then those stomach contents and the milk will go into the lungs and cause what we call an aspiration pneumonia.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So unlike aspiration out of the body completely by a tube, this is within the body?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: There's aspiration upwards, essentially --
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- and the risk is going into the lungs and effectively drowning the person?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Brearey. Could you remain there and answer any questions asked of you?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Dr Brearey, can I just confirm, in 2015 to 2016, which is the key period that we're dealing with, were you the neonatal lead at the Countess of Chester neonatal unit?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And did you continue in that role in the period that followed that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Up to 2020.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. Just so we understand, the neonatal lead is the clinician whose role is -- it's an administrative role involved with the governance and management on the unit; is that correct?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: As well as being a practising clinician too?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Clearly you spend more time dealing with neonatal issues, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So as neonatal lead, your role with the unit was to be responsible for administration and management?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but some of that management would include guideline developments, looking at clinical risk, incident review, that sort of thing, which were clinical areas that I was involved with.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. Thank you. I'm just going to ask a few questions about [Baby G]; other areas of background we can deal with on another occasion.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: At the time that this happened and [Baby G] experienced the events that you've described, your view at that point was that
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: infection was the most likely cause of her sudden collapse and further deterioration. That's what you thought then, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's what I... On the night you want to do everything you can for [Baby G] to preserve life and make her better, and infection would have been a differential diagnosis.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Immediately afterwards -- I'm looking at the CRP results that came back -- my initial impression was that it was infection, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right. You've described the problems that [Baby G] encountered with breathing, or with respiration, while she was on the ventilator, you've described that. And one of the things that took place was the ventilator was changed, wasn't it, to see if that would assist with the breathing?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I didn't describe a problem with breathing, I described a problem with oxygenation on the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. One of the problems you described was oxygenation and what you did or one of things that was done was to change the ventilator to see if that improved oxygenation?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: As it happened, that didn't seem to improve oxygenation, did it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: But we've seen, we can look at the notes if you like -if we stay on the section that we had, please, Mr Murphy, and go to page 6544 on the tile that we were looking at, the composite tile.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we look down the page, we can see "ETT removed", can you see, about five lines down?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: "ETT removed at 06.10."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was the endotracheal tube that had been used on both ventilators, wasn't it? That was the arrangement?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Yes. So when there was the problem with oxygenation on the first ventilator, that was the tube that was being used, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And when the problem with oxygenation continued on the second ventilator, that was the tube that was being used, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When the tube was removed it was seen there were "thick secretions ++" in the mouth and a blood clot on the end of the tube. And that blood clot was something that was capable of interfering with air passing down the tube, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It might interfere with it, but it wouldn't have blocked it completely.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: No, but that could play a part in the interference with oxygenation, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The gases that were done prior to those desaturations didn't show a problem, so it might have had a small degree of influence but I wouldn't consider that to be significant in causing the desaturation that was seen.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Do you remember how big the clot was? Do you remember it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I can't, no.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You weren't there, were you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The only person that saw the clot was Dr Ventress.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's right. So a blood clot of sufficient size could block the end of an ETT, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I have never come across that in practice. The nature of a ventilator is that it's pushing pressure of 26 centimetres of water down an ET tube, so that the natural history of having any clot there would be that -- a clot isn't sticky enough to completely occlude an ET tube because you have 26 centimetres of pressure pushing the clot out of the way.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Well, it was on the end of it, wasn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: It was on the end of it, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: So it hadn't been pushed out of the way, had it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, but on the end of it doesn't mean completely occluding the internal diameter of the ET tube.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: The fact is you don't know how it was positioned on the end of the ET tube, do you, Dr Brearey?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: None of us do.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Well, Dr Ventress might; she was there.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, she saw the clot but that's after she took the tube out.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Anyway, you agree, you don't actually know what position it was in, do you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: In my experience, when there's been blood in the airway previously, I've never come across a clot forming around the tube so it completely occludes it.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Anyway, I'm not going to repeat what I've asked about that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: The aspirate that was removed, 100ml, we can see that referred to there. You've described that as -- you said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "I assume that was milk/stomach fluid contents."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That is what you said, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Looking at what we've got on the note there, do we see any reference to milk, fluid or stomach contents?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: No. You said it's surprising to find fluid like that.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Mm-hm.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That would be surprising to you, would it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It would be abnormal to find fluid like that in the circumstances, would you say?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Of course you were present at this point, weren't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I was.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: When you were asked about this, the prosecution also just now referred to this as being 100ml of fluid that was aspirated --
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's correct.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: -- in light of what you said. Do you remember in fact what it was that was aspirated that comprised that 100ml?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Well, the only other possibility, if it's not stomach contents or milk, would be blood, and I certainly don't recall 100ml of blood being aspirated because that would have been so unusual and abnormal that it would have been recorded by somebody.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It could be air actually, couldn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: It couldn't be?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No because you're not -- you're aspirating fluid, you don't aspirate air from a syringe.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: If something surprising came out and it was worthy of comment, you would expect that to be recorded, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And this doesn't say what it is that was aspirated, does it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because there can only either be milk or stomach contents that you're aspirating.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If you're just getting air back -- quite often -- the process of aspirating prior to intubation is the NG tube that comes out of the stomach is taped to the side of the baby's face. The nurse connects the syringe to the NG tube and pulls back. If they just pull back air then that would be deemed to be not significant and not recorded. They'd only record something if they're pulling back fluid.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: You have been asked to comment and been taken to what Dr Ventress says in the notes so I think it's only fair we remind ourselves of what she said in evidence about this when the prosecution asked her questions.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was asked about the aspirate, she said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: It's quite common when you're giving the breathing support via the mask for their tummies to get bigger because when you're trying to force air into their lungs, you also force air down into the stomach as well, so it's quite common in that situation that the stomach will get bigger and you would aspirate air out of the stomach."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the prosecutor asked:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: Was it air?"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And Dr Ventress said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I can't say 100% from that. I would think, yes. I haven't documented it so I can't say exactly."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And the prosecutor said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: All right. Do you recall if -- well --"
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: And Dr Ventress said:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: I think I would have documented it if it wasn't air because that would be more unusual."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: She was asked:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Question: Can you tell us anything about the quantity, the 100ml, is that usual or unusual?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "Answer: It's a lot but, as I said, we had been doing that, forcing air in, quite a lot."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: So that's what Dr Ventress said. Her recollection was she couldn't say 100%, but in the circumstances she considered this to be air. Right?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I would agree that -- I wouldn't be able to say 100% but I don't think it would have been recorded if it had been air.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: We've heard what she said and she was a clinician who had been dealing with it throughout.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: If we look at your note, can we move down, please?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Because you have said how surprising this is and you've had something to say to the jury about it in answer to questioning. If we look down at page 6545, you were present during this
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: point. Whatever was going on at the time, we've got your note, you didn't regard this as fit to document in any way, did you, the 100ml? You don't document it, do you, in your note?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: No.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: No. If it was 100ml of fluid, which you have said is surprising and abnormal, you would expect that to be included in your notes, wouldn't you?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes. In retrospect I was concentrating on her care and it would have been easy today, knowing if this was going to court, that I'd recorded that, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Dr Ventress recorded it, didn't she?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes and as I've said, my history is as Dr Ventress' entry at the top of my record, so I had agreed with everything she had already written.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: I have nothing else to ask about that.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Thank you.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Re-examination by MR DRIVER

Just one issue arising: you were asked questions about the blood clot, if it was or may have been blocking or, to use your word, occluding the tube. If that or any substance or object completely blocked or occluded the tube, would the ventilator, the machine, acknowledge that?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Absolutely. There would be an alarm on the ventilator for that.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Sorry, the alarm would sound on the ventilator?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: It would, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Because it's blocked?
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Exactly, yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: And if it wasn't completely blocked but partly blocked, would the capnograph reading be influenced by that?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: The capnograph isn't usually connected when the ventilator is in use. The capnograph is connected in between the endotracheal tube and usually the Neopuff, and usually when babies are on a ventilator for a period of time the capnograph isn't on there, so...
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: That's my error. If the blood clot or any other object or substance partially occluded the airway, short of utter blockage, would the ventilator record that or indicate that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: You might get an impression of that from the flow volume loops that I talked about, which would appear different on the screen of the ventilator.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: Thank you. I have no further questions for you, Dr Brearey.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Does your Lordship have any questions for the witness at this juncture?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: No, I don't. Thank you. But you will be returning. We know that, you know that. So thank you very much for coming and giving evidence to us this morning, Dr Brearey. Would you please not talk to anyone about anything to do with this case and, in particular, your evidence and your involvement in it, but generally about anything to do with this case to preserve the integrity of your evidence.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BREAREY

blocks.text: All right. Thank you very much. You'll be notified when it is that you're required next year.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
My Lord, may I call -- thank you, Dr Brearey -- Dr David Harkness again.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: DR DAVID HARKNESS (recalled)
Examination-in-chief by MR DRIVER
Could you state your name for the record, please?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. It's Dr David Ian Harkness.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: As you've been informed previously, you are still bound by the oath or affirmation that you took when you first gave evidence in this trial. Today we would like to ask you questions about [Baby G]. Do you remember [Baby G]?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Vaguely, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And do you remember seeing [Baby G] on the neonatal unit in the early part of September 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Again, vaguely, but mostly from the clinical notes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And have you had and taken the opportunity to refresh your memory from those notes prior to giving evidence here this morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And do those notes tell you that you were involved in [Baby G]'s care from, at the very latest, 4 September 2015?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Having refreshed your memory, can you, in a sentence or two, tell us how things were with [Baby G] at and around 4 September and the following day or two?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So on 4th she was quite stable. I think from looking through the notes and what I put in my statement she was on lowflow oxygen, so quite a small amount of oxygen that lots of children would go home with. And the main thing that she was requiring was a bit of help with her feeding, so the tube feeds, and she wasn't far off going on to full bottle feeds and going home.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Your statement includes detail but we've just heard that detail from your colleague Dr Brearey as to how she was receiving 180ml per kilogram per day, which is a little greater than the norm and that was designed to add weight to her --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- because she was, we understand and could you confirm, just a little under 2 kilograms in weight at this point in time?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And ideally, is this right, you would prefer babies to be a little heavier than that if they were to be sent home?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. Every unit will have slightly different thresholds. So it tends to be over 2 kilograms, but also, normally, we don't like them to be having the tube feeds when they go home either.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So the feeding regime is important because it's easier and safer for the parents to feed by bottle --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- when unsupervised --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- is that the position? And Dr Brearey told us, and could you confirm, that in terms of general trend, both respiration and here we're focusing upon feeding regimes, things were moving in the right direction --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- generally speaking?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you about 7 September 2015. I'll ask Mr Murphy to put up tile 147, please, and click on the underlying notes.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Your note, Dr Harkness, from 9 am on 7 September.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. We can see your note of her gestational age when born, but the corrected gestational age at this point in time. The problems, could you take us through those briefly, please?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Overnight she'd had a sudden deterioration and we've put "[query] sepsis, [query] aspiration". She'd had -- we knew she already had chronic lung disease, she was ventilated and requiring quite high pressures to help with her lungs. So I think we've got there 26/6, which is pretty high, we'd normally expect it to be 20 or 22.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And there was also some blood seen on intubation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Pausing there, had you had any direct involvement with [Baby G] overnight, as you have called it, perhaps more accurately in the early hours of 7 September?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. This was -- I was on a day shift and this was my first port of call on the morning.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But no doubt you informed yourself of the content of her clinical notes as recorded by Dr Brearey and Dr Ventress --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- previously? So sudden desaturation, part of the narrative. Query sepsis, was that your question or somebody else's question?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: That was the question from overnight.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And what was the basis of pondering that diagnosis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The most likely thing with any deterioration is sepsis, it's the most common occurrence we see in babies, so typically when they deteriorate it'll be one of the first things that we think about.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. How is that investigated?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So we would do bloods to look for the CRP, for the white blood cell count and for blood cultures as well to look for the bacteria in the blood. If stable, we'll do a lumbar puncture, but at this point in time she was far too unwell to do that. Then we also look for the infection, so we would look for -- things like chest X-rays as well tend to be quite common things to do at the time as well.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And how consistently reliable are the blood culture tests designed to discover whether or not sepsis is a factor?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So in a good sample, you do need to make sure you've taken enough blood, then if they are going to be positive, the vast majority will be positive within the first 24 hours.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving to aspiration, is it in your entry as a possible cause of the sudden desaturation?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And in this context, what does that mean, that word?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So aspiration, typically what we mean is that some stomach content or milk from the stomach is brought up, either by -- normally by a vomit and then, instead of being swallowed again, it's breathed in on to the lungs.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So inhaled --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- rather than redigested effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Sorry, next entry.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So CLD is chronic lung disease.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So that's her historic problem --
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: -- as it were, she being a very premature baby?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Ventilated on high pressure." Again, is that the history?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's the position that when I've come in, looking through the notes, the pressures that she needed to push the oxygen into her lungs was higher than I would normally expect a baby that's ventilated.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Blood on intubation." Is this another aspect of your effective shorthand of the preceding note?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. So the next entry, V for ventilation, I anticipate?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We're now moving to your observations?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Could you talk us through them, please.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: SIMV is the type of ventilation mode which gives you breaths as you breathe in. 26 is the pressure that you need to give and, like I said before, about 18 to 22 would be where I would expect. When we get to 26 we're quite worried that the ventilation is not doing what it needs and we're kind of almost at the top end of the range. The 6 is the bit of pressure that helps to keep the lungs open in between breaths. Again, normally we'd go 4 to 5, so 6 is quite high.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The rate or how many breaths we give per minute is 50, which is on the higher side but not too dramatic.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And she's on 60 to 80% -- FiO2 is the amount of oxygen she is requiring to keep her oxygen levels up, which again is high.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So translating that data into words, was she continuing to require and receive a relatively high amount of respiratory support?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: I have put:
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "Continued desaturations and bradycardias."
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So her oxygen levels were still dropping every now and again. That would have been seen from the nursing notes and from the observations chart. And if they drop their oxygen levels for a long point in time, their heart rate slows down, which is the bradycardia. So she's still quite unwell and not doing particularly well from a point of view of her breathing, despite being ventilated.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Pausing there, are you able to assist as to the relative degree of desaturations and bradycardia comparing the presentation at 9 am to that which preceded it in the early hours of the morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Not from there. I'd need to look at the observation charts to make an exact observation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Let's move on then. Tidal volumes?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Tidal volumes is looking at the amount of oxygen that gets into the lungs and expands the lungs. So 7 to 8ml per kilogram is good. What that means is we know that the pressures that we're giving her are expanding the lungs to a good amount, which shows that what we're doing is working to a degree. So that's a good number and means that what we're doing is heading in the right direction.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: F for feeds, is it, next?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. So we understand from Dr Brearey that the plan was to remove her from the feeding regime that she'd been prospering with in the days or weeks prior and now to provide her with assistance intravenously.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And that's effectively your record there, is it?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. CVS?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Cardiovascular system.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How was that performing?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: We'd been struggling with her blood pressure. She's almost a term baby, so the mean blood pressure, the middle blood pressure we'd normally like to be around her gestation, so we'd expect it to be 38 to 40.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: We were struggling to get to those numbers, so 30 to 36 is low, and she was on a medication called dopamine, which should help increase the blood pressure, so actually the fact that she's still got a low blood pressure on medication is quite worrying. Her heart rate was very fast at 200. We'd normally expect it to be in the lower hundreds to up to about 140 to 160 at most. So 200 is very fast. Some of that can be the medication, but also it can mean you are very unwell.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I have put there she's pink, so has good perfusion.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Her urine output, which is the UO, is 0.3ml per kilo per hour. That's very low. It's -- a good measure of how much blood is getting to your organs is how much urine you're able to put out, it means you're getting blood to your kidneys so get the urine out. We normally like that over 1ml per kilo per hour, so 0.3 is worryingly low.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Next entry?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that's CNS, central nervous system.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Dr Brearey informed us that she had effectively been sedated to enable ventilation to perform more effectively. Is that a reflection of that?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So we sedate them and we also give them a muscle relaxant to paralyse them. I have put "no abnormal movements". Sometimes they will have fits. She is not fitting, I have not noticed anything like that. And again the soft spot on her head is soft.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: The next line?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Is haem, which is your kind of -- could be anything to do with blood going around the body. And I have mentioned there was blood seen on intubation, obviously not seen by myself, but this has been mentioned overnight. And we gave her vitamin K. So
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: if you have problems with clotting, the first you think of is, is there a deficiency of vitamin K, so we gave some extra with that, which can help with clotting.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Sepsis?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Sepsis, we put "Re-screened on the 7th", which was from the early hours of the morning.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: "On cefotaxime day 1." That's one of the antibiotics at the time that we gave when we re-screened. The CRP was less than 1, so normal. Her white cell count was 10.1, which is normal. Her neutrophils were 1.4, which is on the lower side, which can suggest infection.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So re-screened to what end?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So that was bloods taken, antibiotics started -- like I said no lumbar puncture at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And the blood results or the results of the analysis of the blood taken, were they indicative of sepsis or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The neutrophils can be low in infection, but not always, so that may be a suggestion, but the fact that the CRP is less than 1 doesn't tie together exactly.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Is this an exact science, as they say?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No, not particularly. CRP can be up and down. There can be a delay to it. Neutrophils, again, can be up and down. If they're less than 1, we're concerned. 1.4 is the lower side but certainly not hugely alarming, but difficult to comment in isolation.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Next, "Bloods"?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Bloods. The sodium, Na, of 132, which is slightly on the low side, and K, the potassium, is 4.7, which is normal.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. The medication -- we've already heard of the medications that were provided and the reasons why. I'm going to invite your attention to the right side of the page above the pagination number J6546.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So lines of three cannulas. I have put cannulae there, the Latin.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Can you tell us what that indicates and what was going on in that regard?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So throughout the course of the night we would have needed to give various medications and when you're on that amount of medications you'll need multiple cannulas to give them because they can't all be given through the same cannula at the same time. So in her case with that many medications she needed multiple cannulas at that point, so she had three in place.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you take us to the next page, Mr Murphy, scrolling down? A continuation of your note, is it, Dr Harkness?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And this entry at the top of the page?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: So I've put on examination she was paralysed and sedated and well perfused, so nice and pink. Her abdomen was soft with no masses. I could hear her bowel sounds.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Her abdomen was quite distended. Her femoral pulses were strong and present bilaterally.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And so you arrived at the following plan?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: The PEEP, the lower number on the ventilation, we have dropped to 5. Sometimes if it is too high it can interfere, so I have dropped that down to 5. The plan was for an arterial line, which from memory I had several attempts at, but was unsuccessful. Increased the dopamine to 10 micrograms per kilo. She was on a lower dose but because we were struggling with that urine output and the blood pressure, we have increased it. Have discussed with the tertiary centre because she was so unwell and we would be looking at transferring her to Arrowe Park or Liverpool Women's Hospital.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And then the other thing we wanted to check was her clotting with the next set of bloods that we wanted to do, just because she had had the bleeding -- the blood in the intubation overnight.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. I think then we have a slightly later entry from you again at 10 am that morning.
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Yes. So my review there is -- I've mentioned that I have unable to get the arterial line. Her mean blood pressure has now gone up to 52, which is good. Her capillary refill time is 3, so that shows that she's still, although she's pink she's not perfectly perfused.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Her colour has improved, so she's pinker and her peripheries now feel warm, so there is more -- it is giving us an indication
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: that the blood supply is better now the blood pressure is better.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Her blood gas shows a pH of 7.64, which is high.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Her carbon dioxide is 2.74, which is low. The bicarb of 22 is in the normal range. Base excess is still -- is normal. The lactate is 4.3, which is high, so that can show some stress and her getting tired. Glucose of 10.7, which is slightly high, which goes with stress.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And then what I have done is -- my plan is the ventilation is weaned to 24/5, so if the pH is high and the carbon dioxide is low, it suggests that we're now giving too much ventilation and if we overventilate them then that can be risky as well in itself. So we tend to make quite dramatic changes at that point. So we have dropped her top pressure to 24 from 26 and dropped her rate to 40 from 50. So that will slow that breathing down -and carbon dioxide you breathe when you breathe out, so the slower you breathe the more carbon dioxide you will keep in your body. If their carbon dioxide goes higher, then the pH will come down. So that's what I have planned at that point in time. Because we made quite sweeping changes I have then put to repeat the blood gas in 30 minutes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. So taking a step back, having reminded yourself of the detail of your notes from 9 am and 10 am on 7 September, all of which remained, having reviewed the recorded events from the early hours, how was [Baby G] when you examined her on those two occasions an hour apart that morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: She was incredibly sick. She'd stabilised by the point -- by 10 o'clock she was certainly looking better but was still incredibly sick and we were still incredibly worried about her at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And how was her presentation relative to and compared with that recorded by Dr Ventress and Dr Brearey in the earlier hours of the morning?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: Things were improved, but still needing a lot of support and certainly not out of the woods at that point in time.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And was there anything in your observations and examination of and pertaining to [Baby G] that enabled you to diagnose what had happened or not?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: No. The blood tests weren't conclusive of sepsis.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: I can't remember exactly why aspiration was on the list.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: It may well have been extrapolation from the feeds or it may very well have been the X-ray findings, but I have not -- I didn't see those at that point in time. But certainly from what I saw, there was nothing that was concrete that would say this is definitely sepsis or definitely something else.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Would it be exceptional to consider aspiration in this context or is that part of a checklist effectively?
blocks.speaker: DRIVER

blocks.text: It's certainly uncommon. It's certainly not something that we would put in the majority of collapses. It wouldn't be high on our list of concerns.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. Could you remain there and answer any further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: Cross-examination by MR MYERS
Just a couple of points, please, Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: Do you agree that a sudden deterioration, like the sort that [Baby G] had on the night of the 7th, in the early hours of the morning of 7 September 2015, is not uncommon?
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: We see it. It's very rare to see it in an otherwise stable term baby. So I can't say that it's incredibly common, but it does happen.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS
