blocks.text: All right. Just so it's clear where I've got that from, could Dr Harkness be shown his statement? It's at page 1922. So I'm going to ask if you can have a look at this together with his Lordship and the barristers.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: it's page 3 of your statement.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: While we wait to get that, I'll just confirm that this is a statement that you made on 14 September 2018, Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: (Pause)
If we just scroll down a little bit. Can you see you refer to "in respect of 7 September" at the centre of that page, Dr Harkness?
Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And you say that you've referred to your -- "referring to my medical notes entry at 9 am", and then you say this:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G] during the night had a deterioration.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: A sudden deterioration like this is not uncommon.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Subsequently requiring intubation."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how you put it there, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That's how I put it in 2018.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Subsequently, after having -- what was that -- 5 years' further experience and experience as a consultant, from that point to now I would say I've seen considerably less collapses than at that point in time. So I would say unless I changed my statement to reflect my current experience, current experience tells me differently.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: How long had you been practising as a doctor by the time you made your statement in 2018?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: That was 7 years. And that's not uncommon -- that was not referring directly to the gestation of babies. If I was to look through everything from 23 weeks up to term then, if I went into it in more detail, I would say the likelihood goes -decreases as they get older, both in gestation when they're born and gestation from when they're born. So as a point of generalisation I would say it is not be common, but if you were to pin it down to 38 week gestation babies who were otherwise doing incredibly well, I would say that was uncommon.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: So you were 7 years' experienced as a doctor when you wrote that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes, not all in neonatal medicine.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: In any event you agree at the time you wrote that you said a degree of deterioration is not uncommon?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: And in fact, when you came to consider this, your view, Dr Harkness, was there was no surprise to [Baby G]'s deterioration because there's always a risk of infection and the immune systems of a baby like [Baby G] are not established; do you agree with that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Have I written that in my statement?
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: You have and I can take you to it if you like. Could we go over the page to page 4 of 7, so page 1923. Just scroll down
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: that page, please. Just in the centre of that page, just taking the words that you used, Dr Harkness:
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: "[Baby G]'s deterioration on 7 September 2015 was of no surprise to me as this can happen and is relatively common. There is always the risk of infection because their immune systems are not quite established. [Baby G]'s event was not debriefed."
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Do you see that?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: That's what you said then and do you agree that it can be relatively common because their immune systems aren't established and that increases the risk of infection?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly that was my feeling at the time. In hindsight I would say I've seen less and less over time and I would no longer, with my current experience, call it common.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: But your experience then, as a registrar in a busy unit, was that it was common?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Certainly after my time in Chester, I thought that was quite common, yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: No, in your 7 years as a registrar.
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: I wasn't a registrar for 7 years, no, but my experience was 7 years.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Yes. And at that point you felt it was relatively common?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you. To be clear, that is because their immune systems have not established, isn't it?
blocks.speaker: MYERS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: HARKNESS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: MR MYERS

blocks.text: I have no re-examination, my Lord. Does your Lordship have any questions?
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: I don't. Thank you, Dr Harkness.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: Dr Harkness will be coming back.
blocks.speaker: MR DRIVER

blocks.text: So everything I've said before several times still applies. Thank you very much.
blocks.speaker: MR JUSTICE GOSS

blocks.text: (The witness withdrew)
The next witness is Nurse Booth.

blocks.text: So you know, that is satisfactory. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If the jury wouldn't mind keeping open page 7013, and if Mr Murphy would put back up on the screen exhibit AS4, please, which is a photograph.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: At paragraph 32 of your report of 31 May, Dr Evans, you refer specifically to the entry made in the -- by Dr Ventress.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: And you drew certain -- so you quoted it and we've just looked at it. But you expressed a concern in your paragraph 33. Could you tell the jury what your concern is and, in particular, by reference to what [Nurse E] has written there on page 7013?

blocks.text: Well -- 7013, right. We'll start with what [Nurse E] said because she says at 02.00 hours [Baby G] had EBM, expressed breast milk, with fortifier, which is extra calories, less Gaviscon, which is given commonly to little babies, and was given 45ml of feed via nasogastric tube.

blocks.text: Yes. Let's mention that.

blocks.text: The second circle is the one between the chair and the cot on the floor. blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right. Let's just -- sorry to stop you, but if Mr Murphy could help us by reminding us of what Lucy Letby wrote down at tile 79, please. If we can go to the original note behind the tile, please.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So:
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: "[Baby G] had large projectile milky vomit at 2.15, continued to vomit ++. 45ml milk obtained from NG tube with air ++. Abdomen noted to be distended and discoloured. Colour improved few minutes after aspirating tube, remained distended but soft.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Reg Ventress asked to review. To go nil by mouth with IV fluids."
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So just going back to your report then, please, Dr Evans, with my apologies for stopping you and referring the jury back to Lucy Letby's note, could you continue your explanation?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, if I continue on my paragraph 33, really.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So the entry from (inaudible) makes it clear the member of staff aspirated 45ml of feed from the NG tube in addition to the milk she had vomited. There can be only one explanation: [Baby G] had received more, far more, than 45ml of feed down the NG tube before she vomited at 02.15 hours. She may also have received a bolus of air from the feeding syringe used for feeding. This caused the abdominal distension, the distress, the change of abdomen colour and the vomiting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, just to add to that, just one thing, really. So [Baby G] must have received far, far more milk down the tube. She probably had more air as well. And given that it had caused the abdominal distension, et cetera, I don't think this got down by gravity, so the mechanical explanation is that the plunger end of the syringe must have been put over the syringe and the milk forced down, squirted down the tube, if you like, using a syringe, and this caused the baby -- would have caused the abdominal distension to start off with, then it would have caused the baby distress and, of course, she would have vomited because of the gross overdistension of her stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So given that you've told us that in the absence of pyloric stenosis -- well, let's deal with pyloric stenosis first before I ask you this question. Why do you exclude that as a possibility for what happened?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, pyloric stenosis is something that occurs with babies 6 to 8 weeks of age or thereabouts and it doesn't occur and disappear, it requires a surgical procedure to treat the overgrown muscle at the bottom of the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Therefore if she had pyloric stenosis the vomiting would have continued until somebody took her to theatre and operated on her.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Can we exclude that as a possibility?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: We can exclude pyloric stenosis completely.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: You have told us that baby of this size and age would be incapable of producing the amount of force required to vomit out of the cot on to the floor and beyond on to a chair.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Mm.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So what's the physical explanation for how this baby undoubtedly did manage to do that?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, she -- well, right. The whole of the gastrointestinal system has a series of muscles, from the mouth all the way through. A particular kind of muscle is called smooth muscle. Muscles only go one way, therefore milk will go from the mouth down through the oesophagus, through the stomach, through the intestine and then out the other end. So it's oneway traffic.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The only time this does not work is if the baby's compromised by something. Okay? So in this situation the baby was compromised by receiving a large volume of fluid into the stomach, and in that situation, the stomach muscles would contract and the contraction of the stomach muscles would lead to the baby vomiting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: This is not unique to babies. If anybody drank too much fluid too quickly, you'd end up with a similar pattern of vomiting. So therefore the mechanism of it is straightforward.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is it like putting a large amount of air or fluid, or a combination, into a balloon to stretch the balloon and then letting your fingers off the end in effect?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Is that the sort of idea?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I'd make it simpler than that.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Go on.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'd make it simpler than that. You can't be flippant in this. But if an adult drank a large volume of liquid too quickly they would probably vomit --
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: -- because there is a rate at which liquid can go from stomach to intestines through to the intestine, therefore any indulgence of drink leads to vomiting.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Okay.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The stomach muscles contract and it all comes out.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So this is what happened to this little baby.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on to your paragraph 35, Dr Evans.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you look at the X-rays of [Baby G] and, in particular, one that was timed just before 5 am at --
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I did. Now, I emphasise I'm not a radiologist, so we do have a radiology opinion, but obviously I'm familiar with looking at X-rays of the abdomens and chests of little babies, so this is about the limit of my radiology competence as it were. And the X-rays shows chronic lung disease and a great deal of air in the abdomen, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: We'll leave that for the radiologists in due course.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Thereafter, so far as this report was concerned, were there -did you come to any conclusions about what happened to [Baby G] following this unusual vomit at anything between 2.15 and 2.30?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, I did. Her condition over the next few hours was incredibly unstable. I'll explain it in more detail, but this is a time when she's experienced a significant amount of oxygen deprivation. There are recorded values of oxygen saturations 40% and 50% and also bradycardia, heart rate down, and also lowish blood pressure. So therefore, getting [Baby G] back to where she was before 2 am turned out to be extremely challenging and extremely difficult. They did get her round because obviously she survived, but she suffered sufficient oxygen deprivation to cause significant irreversible brain damage.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: And her resuscitation was quite difficult. I've heard Dr Ventress' testimony and Dr Brearey. So it was quite difficult for all, and I just mention one or two things.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The first thing that Dr Ventress mentioned was when she tried to intubate the baby, in other words you put a laryngoscope into the back of the throat to get a tube in, an endotracheal tube, she noticed blood. She noticed blood not just at the back of the throat but the other side, in other words on the lung side of the vocal cords.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: So in other words, there was bleeding. Now, this doesn't mean -- this doesn't... The fact there was blood beyond the vocal cords, in other words towards the lungs, doesn't mean that the bleeding came from beyond the cords, it could be that the bleeding came from the upper -- from the back of the throat and, you know, and then trickled down through the cords. You can't say one way or the other.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: But certainly there was bleeding there and the important thing about the bleeding is that this was found at the initial resuscitation. So in other words although they had tremendous difficulties with ventilation, the bleeding was not noted an hour later or with a second intubation or with a third intubation.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And the significance of that is this: that the bleeding was there from the first time that the baby was -- from the first occasion that resuscitation with intubation was attempted.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And we know that [Baby G] did not have a bleeding disorder, in other words she was not at increased risk of haemorrhage or bleeding. So therefore, the bleeding was present from the beginning. And I think Dr Harkness said the same thing: there was blood at the back of the throat, so there was bleeding at the back of the throat from more or less the time that [Baby G] crashed/collapsed.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is this the same sort of bleeding we've seen so far in any other case so far as you can tell or is it different?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. Well, we've seen this before, but much worse in little [Baby E]. That's case number 5, the first of the twins. But the bleeding that we found there was much worse, he lost a third of his blood. So the bleeding here was not major. But the fact that it was present is not something that one would normally expect and it cannot be explained on the basis of vomiting only.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: No. The possibility of pulmonary haemorrhage, so bleeding from the lungs, do you regard that as being a realistic source of the blood in this particular case?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, I do not. Pulmonary haemorrhage is a killer and if the haemorrhage was in the lungs itself, she's unlikely to have survived, quite frankly. But she certainly wouldn't have picked up -- although she took several hours to pick up, I don't think she'd have picked up in such a short period of time. So I don't think pulmonary haemorrhage was a factor in this collapse at all.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So far as the issue of infection is concerned, from your interpretation of what happened did you regard infection as being a credible explanation for [Baby G]'s vomiting and collapse some time after 2 am?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, not at all. [Baby G]'s infection, in my opinion, occurred after the collapse. I think it is worth explaining this in some detail because it applies -- it's applied to previous
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: babies and it will apply to babies we're going to be discussing later.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The key thing is that when babies start to sicken for an infection, nursing and medical staff in baby units are alert to subtle changes. So the oxygen requirement may go up, the oxygen saturation may go down. The breathing may become a little bit irregular.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They generally don't -- they're not quite as well as they should be. There's none of that. There's none of that. There is this complete stability. You might get pooling of blood -- sorry, pooling of milk in the stomach. That did not occur. We know that she was on 45ml every 3 hours and all of it was going through either by bottle or by NG tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore there were no markers of infection clinically at all. And then 2 hours, nearly 2 hours after her collapse, the blood tests we've discussed showed a CRP of less than 1 and a neutrophil count of 1.4. Normal.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Now, we know that CRP is not always increased at the presentation of infection, but it is in -- it is more likely than not to be increased. But the other thing that's important in [Baby G]'s case is that her infection, if I could put it that way, was very CRP relevant. In other words, her CRPs really shot up. So 12 hours later, it was 28, which is not particularly high.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: 20 hours or so later, it was 106, and I think there was a value of over 200 later on after she'd been transferred.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So therefore, none of her clinical features indicate infection. None of the blood tests indicate infection.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So in my opinion, the infection occurred after the resuscitation, most likely, and this is not a criticism by the way, most likely in association with all the efforts they made to get her going, you know, to save her life, really. So there we are.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Moving on, if we may, and I'm moving on, Dr Evans, to a later report of yours, please, of 17 October 2021 and I'm looking specifically at your paragraph 7, which is, I think, your page 5, if your print is as mine appears on the screen.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: My response to the 10 questions?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Correct, yes. I think you were asked to consider Dr Ventress' suggestion that [Baby G]'s initial collapse, when she
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: projectile vomited and 45ml of milk was aspirated from her stomach, you were asked to consider whether that was consistent with being the product of an infection.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: With respect to Dr Ventress, no, I don't agree with that. I think the infection occurred afterwards.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes. Is that for the reasons that you have already explained?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, yes, yes. And of course, infection would not cause a baby to vomit halfway across the nursery. And where would the extra fluid come from? Because even after vomiting, they aspirated 45ml of milk from the stomach, so therefore she had only been fed 45ml. So if you are fed 45ml, some of the milk will have already gone through the stomach into the duodenum, you're not going to aspirate every millilitre anyway because, you know, you can't aspirate 100%, but they still aspirated 45ml.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They also aspirated air. Where on earth did the air come from? Plus all the vomit on the chair and on the floor and everywhere else. So therefore, she must have had far, far more volume of milk than 45ml.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. Now, one of the things you were asked to deal with on the issue of air was something that Lucy Letby told the police when she was interviewed.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Ah, right.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I'm now looking at your paragraph 7 at page 7 of your report, it's the same report, 17 October. So the suggestion made by Lucy Letby in her interview was that an explanation for there being a lot of air in [Baby G] was that when babies vomit they swallow a lot of air.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, they don't. They don't. I mean, you'll vomit -- air will come out with liquid. It won't go back in.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Therefore if a baby doesn't swallow large quantities of air, what conclusion did you draw as to how the air got there that was aspirated with the milk?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Right. As far as the initial one is concerned, I think as well as having quite a lot of additional milk pushed down into the nasogastric tube, I think she had excess air as well down that tube, and that contributed to the abdominal distension. So she had air down the tube and excess milk down the tube.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And so far as Dr Brearey's evidence -- we have had differing versions of the 100ml aspiration from Dr Ventress and Dr Brearey as to whether or not it was air or whether it was fluid, possibly milk. But would infection account for either as far as you are concerned?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, no. I have never seen a baby with an infection present in this way. You know, it's just not the way they present.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: All right. I think at a later stage -- and I'm looking now, Dr Evans, at your report of 22 April 2022, 22/4/22 -- you were asked about whether or not it was normal for babies who are fed via NGTs to vomit at all.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, they don't.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: It's your paragraph 4.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, they don't. Because what -- you see, it has been explained before, but I'm not sure it's been explained clearly enough. When you have a baby on nasogastric feeds, the nurse will put a syringe before the feed -- before the feed the nurse will put a syringe on to the top of the nasogastric tube and aspirate, in other words suck back from the syringe to see if there's any residual milk there.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: They do it for two reasons: first of all, to see if there's residual milk because if the milk -- if there's a fair bit of milk from a previous feed that has not gone through, then you need to be careful about giving more milk. The second reason they aspirate the tube is to measure the acidity of the stomach content, and the reason they do that is to ensure that the end of the nasogastric tube is actually in the stomach. Okay?
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The stomach has acid. Nasogastric tubes can come out and can go down the wrong way, go into the lung, so the last thing you want to do is to give milk into the wrong orifice, into the lung. Therefore, the reason that they measure pH before each feed is to ensure that the tip of the nasogastric tube is actually in the stomach.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: If the baby is on bottle feed then you don't need to do that because obviously the baby will swallow normally and the milk will go down the right hole, into the stomach. But with nasogastric feeding you must ensure as a nurse that the nasogastric tube tip is in the stomach and this is why you measure its pH and a pH of 4, acid, tube in the correct place.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you. Can I turn finally, please, to your report of 22 April 2022 and to really the conclusion of that report, please. I'm looking at paragraph 12.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: I'll just read it. This is my last paragraph:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "Inserting an excessive volume of fluid/milk via nasogastric tube with or without associated air cannot occur accidentally. A professional member of staff, nursing or medical, who gives a small baby an excessive volume of milk places that infant in harm's way. It places the infant at risk of vomiting and the complication of aspiration pneumonia. Excessive volume of fluid in the stomach also interferes with diaphragm movement, splinting the diaphragm..."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Meaning the diaphragm can't move up and down:
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: "... leading to the risk of respiratory distress, respiratory failure and cardiorespiratory collapse."
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that was my final...
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So the diaphragm is the very strong muscle under the lungs; is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct, yes.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: And as the diaphragm moves, it reduces pressure in the lungs, which draws in air?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Is that right?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Correct.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: The effect of the stomach being overfull of air and/or fluid has what effect on that movement of the diaphragm?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: If the stomach is full of fluid, the diaphragm cannot move down. The diaphragm needs to move down to suck air in. If the diaphragm cannot move down because the stomach is full of air, then the baby cannot receive air and oxygen into its lungs, and it'll lead very rapidly to oxygen deprivation, oxygen reduction, in other words oxygen saturations falling, followed by bradycardia, in other words heart rate falling, followed by collapse.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: So that's the mechanism of a sequence of this nature.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: I think we'll hear about that at a later time with another baby. But as far as [Baby G] is concerned, this is what compromised her.
blocks.speaker: EVANS

blocks.text: Thank you, Dr Evans. Would you wait there, please, for some further questions?
blocks.speaker: MR JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: -- in those 2 days?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: That's correct.

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Did you, in your opinion and observations of your report, conclude that [Baby G] was very vulnerable, born at the margins of viability?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: And that she had a very stormy early neonatal course, which required a huge amount of neonatal intensive care?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes, that's correct.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Having looked at the material from Chester in its entirety, which of course includes the material we've just referred to, what conclusions did you draw as to her state of health up to the point at which she collapsed some time after 2 am on 7 September?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: She was very stable at that time. She had -- her respiratory requirements had changed from CPAP to high flow and then to a very small amount of low-flow oxygen.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: She did have chronic lung disease, which meant that her lungs were abnormal, but she was managing well on a small amount of oxygen. Her respiratory rate was stable, her oxygen saturation was stable. She wasn't having any desaturations. So from the respiratory point of view, all was well. Her heart rate was stable, her temperature was stable.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: On top of that she had gone from two-hourly feeds to threehourly feeds over the course of the time at the Countess of Chester and was tolerating those. She'd started taking some bottles and therefore things were progressing really very well and as you'd expect them to be for a term baby.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Thank you. I'm looking at your paragraph 7.3, but if the jury want to remind themselves of the observation charts that are at the beginning of divider 7. What conclusions did you draw from what you could see on the charts as to [Baby G]'s vital signs before the first of the collapses?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: They were all completely normal.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So far as the report of projectile vomiting is concerned and the photograph marked by and the description given by Ailsa Simpson is concerned, what conclusions or views did you reach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: The whole episode was concerning for me. Ailsa Simpson said that they heard projectile vomiting so I'm not quite sure what they heard because when babies vomit it's usually silent,
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: but maybe they heard the vomit hitting the floor. In my experience, even working on a neonatal surgical unit, I haven't seen babies of 2 kilograms projectile vomiting. So for me that was something that was quite extraordinary.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Putting that into the context of the distance of the vomit, together with the fact that 45ml of milk was aspirated together with air plus plus, what conclusion did you reach?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Well, there must be a huge volume of milk coming from somewhere because the baby's generated a huge amount of force in order to projectile vomit. It wasn't only on the cot but over the side of what is quite a deep side to the cot that we were shown that she was being nursed in at the time. So a baby lying flat on their back has to vomit over the side of the cot, which gets to the floor and then over the side again to get on to the chair. And in order to move that distance, a considerable force has to be generated within the abdomen. We don't know the volume of that vomit. But it was clearly a lot if it's landed in three places and on top of that the nurses write, "Continued to vomit ++", whatever that means, and there's 45ml of milk aspirated from the stomach. So altogether there must have been at some point much more than 45ml of milk within the stomach.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: Yes. In your view, is there a credible "innocent"
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: explanation for there being more than 45ml of milk in [Baby G]'s stomach at the time that she vomited?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No, because I think her stomach was empty prior to that 2 o'clock feed because the pH was 4. If she'd had a lot of milk in her stomach (a) the nurse who aspirated it to test the pH would have noted that -- she may not have wanted to aspirate the whole lot, but she would have noted that there was milk in the stomach, and she hasn't noted that, but what she has noted is that the pH is 4.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: If there was milk in the stomach the pH would not have been 4, that's very acidic. The pH would have buffered -- the milk would have buffered the acid in the stomach so would have neutralised it to some extent and you wouldn't have got a pH of 4.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: So there was additional milk. The additional milk that is vomited had to have come from somewhere.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: I think her stomach was empty and I think the only plausible explanation for me was that she was given an excessive amount of milk, and possibly air, down the nasogastric tube, which distended her stomach and caused her to then vomit in the way she did.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In this context we have heard, and you have been listening in, watching in via the video facility, we've heard about [Baby G]'s CRP level being normal just before the incident, getting to the margins of normality at 12, or whatever it was, a bit later, and then increasing to a figure of over 100 by the late evening of the same day.
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: Yes.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.text: In your view, is what happened to [Baby G] plausibly explained by an infection?
blocks.speaker: JOHNSON

blocks.text: No. I think it's clear that [Baby G] had an infection, but I don't think the projectile vomit heralded the start of the infection. That isn't the way that infections present in neonates of this age and size. They usually provide the carers with subtle markers that all is not well and she showed none of those things. Starting with a huge projectile vomit and then continuing to deteriorate in the way she did is not the way that infection presents.
blocks.speaker: BOHIN

blocks.speaker: JOHNSON
